claims.text: CrFeCoNiX alloys can exist as single- or multiphase metallic solid solutions with homogeneous elemental distributions.
Formation of a stable, coherent, slow-growing oxide above 900 °C is governed by the identity and content of X and its interaction with Cr.
An appropriate X element promotes formation of a mixed Cr–X oxide.
The protective mixed Cr–X oxide has a Pilling–Bedworth ratio near unity.
The protective mixed oxide has thermal-expansion characteristics similar to those of the alloy substrate.
A near-unity Pilling–Bedworth ratio minimizes volumetric mismatch and stress accumulation in the oxide scale.
Low thermal-expansion mismatch reduces interfacial stress between the oxide and substrate.
Reduced interfacial stress prevents oxide-scale cracking and spallation.
The Cr–X interaction promotes nucleation and growth of the proposed mixed oxide film.
The continuous mixed Cr–X scale mediates oxidation protection.
Alloys containing an appropriate amount of X will form a slow-growing, adherent oxide that remains intact during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Alloys lacking the optimized Cr–X interaction, or containing an unfavorable X combination, will develop internally stressed oxides that crack or spall.
The proposed mechanism remains operative during thermal cycling.
Thermal-expansion mismatch is the dominant scale-failure factor within the stated service boundary.
Avoiding segregated intermetallics prevents extrinsic microstructural effects on oxide adhesion.
The comparison will systematically vary X content and identity while including a control lacking the optimized X contribution.
A lack of composition-dependent cracking or spallation, or a lack of correlation with Pilling–Bedworth ratio and thermal-expansion mismatch, would falsify the hypothesis.
